statement: Distinguishes four boundary types -- physical boundary (system X), semantic boundary (concept C), epistemic boundary (what agent A can currently distinguish), and institutional boundary (context C where X counts as Y) -- as part of solving the project's ongoing 'boundary' problem.

anchor: Person -> counts-as Voter -> votes -> counts-as Candidate/Election outcome -> counts-as Winner -> counts-as President -> has Power -> can Appoint -> new Institutional Status
statement: Analyzes Searle's discussion of iterated status functions and interlocking systems (a status can itself become the basis for another status), applying it to an election chain (Person -> Voter -> Candidate/outcome -> Winner -> President -> Power -> Appoint -> new Institutional Status) to argue the Knowledge Space is not a flat graph but has iterated institutional structure.

anchor:
### Natural relation

```text
causes
contains
touches
located-in
```
statement: Classifies relations into four kinds -- natural (causes/contains/touches/located-in), semantic (means/refers-to/predicates/represents), epistemic (supports/contradicts/believes/knows/justifies), and institutional (counts-as/authorizes/requires/permits/obligates/appoints/owns/certifies) -- described as one of the cleanest classifications reached so far.

anchor:
I would now **not** put all these relations into one generic:

```text Relation
```
statement: Argues against putting all relation kinds into one generic Relation type at the conceptual level, proposing instead a meta-level RELATIONAL SUBSTRATE with natural/semantic/epistemic/institutional branches, so the Kernel can preserve typed relations without prescribing all domain semantics -- described as a much safer architecture.

anchor: # 28. Searle also reinforces our "preserve history, project state" model
statement: Reinforces the project's 'preserve history, project state' model using Searle's account that institutional facts persist only so long as relevant institutional acceptance/recognition and structures continue: Institutional State at t is derived from constitutional rules + status assignments + collective recognition + institutional events + history, adding Institutional State -> Knowledge about Institutional State to the existing History -> projection -> Knowledge State chain.

anchor: report of decision ... from ... decision that constitutes institutional change
statement: Argues a governance decision is not only a report-of-decision assertion but may be a decision event that constitutes a status-function assignment producing a new institutional status and new rights/obligations/powers; proposes KnowledgeOS distinguish these two cases as a potentially major architectural invariant.

anchor: Not all projections are projections of the same kind of reality. Some project natural facts; some project semantic structures; some project institutional statuses; some project epistemic states.
statement: Refines the per-agent projection model (from S0529/S0530) by arguing not all projections project the same kind of reality -- some project natural facts, some semantic structures, some institutional statuses, some epistemic states -- and that KnowledgeOS must preserve which kind of projection a given projection is, calling this a major boundary condition.

anchor: Is it: a person? a status? an institutional role? a relation? a power-bearing position? a concept? a proposition? an epistemic object?
statement: Argues against a single generic KnowledgeObject using 'President' as a worked ambiguity example (depending on context it may be a person, a status, an institutional role, a relation, a power-bearing position, a concept, a proposition, or an epistemic object), proposing instead that KnowledgeOS preserve the underlying structures (person, status function, context, institution, constitutive rule, authority, time, rights/obligations, evidence) so different projections ('X is President', 'X has presidential authority', 'X was President from T1 to T2') can be expressed without losing the underlying structure -- called exactly the kind of semantic integrity being sought.

anchor:
McGinn
  │
  └── Identity / Existence / Predication / Truth / Modality
statement: Synthesizes the whole six-book research arc into one table (McGinn: Identity/Existence/Predication/Truth/Modality; Floridi: Levels of Abstraction/Observables/Relevance; Dretske: Information/Transmission/Possibility reduction; Fagin: Agents/Epistemic states/Shared knowledge; Gardenfors: Expansion/Revision/Contraction/Entrenchment; Searle: Social reality/Status/Institutions/Collective intentionality/Deontic powers) and a boxed chain: Infinite Knowledge Space -> Reality/Semantics/Institutions -> Observations -> Epistemic States -> Projections.

anchor: This book should materially influence the KnowledgeOS model.
statement: States an architectural verdict that Searle's book should materially influence the KnowledgeOS model, identifying Status(X,Y,C)/status-assignment-under-context (not 'Institution' as a class) as the biggest new addition, applicable to roles, elections, mandates, offices, authority, rights, obligations, ownership, certification, governance, and constitutional status/boundaries, because institutional facts form interlocking systems, persist through collective recognition, and can be created by authorized/constitutive acts.

anchor: Knowledge Space contains not only a world of objects and events and a space of propositions and epistemic states, but also a socially/institutionally constructed space of statuses, powers, obligations and roles whose existence depends on rules and collective recognition.
statement: States the key Zero-Lens conclusion of the file: the Knowledge Space contains not only a world of objects/events and a space of propositions/epistemic states, but also a socially/institutionally constructed space of statuses, powers, obligations and roles whose existence depends on rules and collective recognition, and that this institutional space must remain distinguishable from the underlying natural facts and from knowledge of both.

anchor: knowledge = capacity to write information
statement: Rejects the proposed formulation 'knowledge = capacity to write information' as too narrow, on the grounds that a person can know something without being able to write it down, and an institutional system can preserve information without 'knowing' it in the epistemic sense.

anchor: So **capacity** sits between the infinite space and the particular knowledge projection.
statement: Formalizes a four-stage chain separating Infinite Knowledge Space -> Information (via encounter/observation) -> Knowledge Capacity (via select/interpret/relate/evaluate) -> Knowledge Projection (within a defined scope), placing 'capacity' as an intermediate layer between the infinite space and any particular knowledge projection.

anchor: what can be represented
statement: Lists what Knowledge Capacity determines: what can be represented, what can be distinguished, what can be connected, what can be justified, what can be communicated, and what can be acted upon.

anchor: Floridi gives us the idea that a representation is made at a selected **Level of Abstraction**, with a selected set of observables.
statement: Ties the Knowledge Capacity construct back to all four prior book-lenses: Floridi's Level-of-Abstraction/observables defines what portion of a system can be represented; Gärdenfors' epistemic state contains commitments and changes through inputs/expansion/revision/contraction; Dretske separates information from its physical/linguistic encoding, so the capacity to 'write' information is not identical to the information itself; Searle adds that some information participates in institutional structures where context determines what something counts as.

anchor: K = (B, L, R, C, P)
statement: Formalizes Knowledge Capacity as the tuple K=(B,L,R,C,P) where B=boundary, L=level of abstraction, R=epistemic/reasoning regime, C=contextual capacity, P=participant/system capacity, producing a Knowledge Projection K(Omega) over the unbounded Knowledge Space Omega.
type_signature: K = (B, L, R, C, P); Knowledge Projection = K(Omega)

anchor: Knowledge is not only what is contained in the projection; it is also the capability and boundary that determine what can enter the projection.
statement: States that knowledge is not only what is contained in a projection but also the capability and boundary that determine what can enter the projection in the first place.

anchor: ## That gives us three different capacities
statement: Distinguishes three separate capacities: (1) information capacity -- how much information can be captured or represented (storage, bandwidth, memory, sensor resolution); (2) epistemic capacity -- what the participant can distinguish, infer, justify, revise or understand (reasoning, awareness, inference, uncertainty handling, causal understanding); (3) expressive capacity -- what the participant can communicate or externalize (language, symbols, documents, models, code, diagrams).

anchor:
high epistemic capacity
low expressive capacity
statement: Gives worked capacity profiles illustrating the three-capacity distinction: a person may have high epistemic capacity but low expressive capacity, or high storage capacity but low epistemic capacity; an LLM may have high expressive capacity and large representational capacity but uncertain epistemic capacity; a database may have high preservation capacity but almost no intrinsic epistemic capacity.

anchor: KnowledgeOS preserves and exposes the structures through which a participant can construct, scope, represent, evaluate, relate, revise, and communicate a projection of the infinite Knowledge Space.
statement: Proposes a revised definition of KnowledgeOS, replacing 'KnowledgeOS stores knowledge' with 'KnowledgeOS preserves and exposes the structures through which a participant can construct, scope, represent, evaluate, relate, revise, and communicate a projection of the infinite Knowledge Space' -- concluding the Kernel does not need to contain 'knowledge' but needs to preserve the conditions and history of knowledge projection.

anchor: Knowledge is a capacity to construct and maintain a bounded, meaningful projection of an unbounded Knowledge Space by selecting, relating, evaluating, preserving, and expressing information within a context and purpose.
statement: Offers a further-refined single-sentence definition of knowledge: 'Knowledge is a capacity to construct and maintain a bounded, meaningful projection of an unbounded Knowledge Space by selecting, relating, evaluating, preserving, and expressing information within a context and purpose,' replacing the earlier 'capacity to write information and define the scope of information' formulation.

anchor: Is 'capacity' itself a Kernel primitive, or is capacity derived from the participant, boundary, representation, epistemic regime, and available resources?
statement: Leaves open whether 'capacity' itself is a Kernel primitive or is fully derived from participant + boundary + representation + epistemic regime + available resources, naming it the next question the Zero Lens should test.
dependencies: Zero Lens elimination test methodology (S0511, S0512)
